title: Reconstructionist Judaism
hookLine: Mordecai Kaplan described Judaism as an evolving religious civilization

cards: One shelf in a family's living room. A prayer book with a cracked spine. A cookbook with honey cake stains on the page for the new year.
A record of old Yiddish songs. A Hebrew newspaper someone brought back from a trip. A history of the family's town that no longer exists.
A pair of Shabbat candlesticks. Which of these things is Judaism? Only the prayer book?
Or the whole shelf? A teacher named Mordecai Kaplan gave an answer that started a movement.

teach.b: Kaplan was a rabbi and a teacher, and his answer was: the whole shelf. Judaism, he wrote, is not only a religion, a set of beliefs and rituals.
It is a civilization: the whole life of a people, including its language, its land, its history, its literature, its art and music, its food, its customs and its law.
Religion is at its heart, he said, but it is not the whole of it. Three words carry the idea. First, civilization.
If Judaism is a civilization, then a Jew who sings the songs, studies the history, speaks Hebrew or cooks the holiday foods is taking part in Jewish life, not standing outside it. Second, evolving.
Civilizations change; they borrow, adapt and grow. Kaplan argued that Judaism always has, and has to keep doing it to stay alive.

That is where the name comes from: each generation reconstructs the tradition for its own time, the way you might rebuild an old house, keeping the foundation and changing the rooms. Third, the people.
Kaplan put the Jewish people at the center, the community that carries the civilization forward.
A psalm pictures that handing-on: "One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts." Each one receives, and each one builds.
Kaplan taught within the Conservative world for a long time, and Reconstructionism grew from his ideas into a movement of its own.

how: Reconstructionist Jews, following Mordecai Kaplan, treat Judaism as the evolving civilization of the Jewish people, so congregations embrace Jewish culture, language, history and arts alongside prayer and ritual.

games.q: you're Kaplan, looking at the family's shelf. which of these things is Judaism?
o: the prayer book and the candlesticks, nothing else.
games.why: Kaplan's answer was the whole shelf: Judaism is a civilization, with religion at its heart, but including language, history, art, food and customs.

practice: Picture the shelf again, and let each thing come forward, one at a time: the prayer book, the recipe, the song, the story of a town, the candlesticks, all belonging to the same people. Then, if you like, turn to your own life.
What would be on your shelf, and which things there carry a whole civilization?

wordCard.voice: Reconstructionist Judaism. The movement built on Mordecai Kaplan's idea that Judaism is an evolving religious civilization, rebuilt by each generation. Today's word.
